questions.prompt: When should you reach for a tall fractional distillation column instead of a basic simple distillation flask?
choices: Whenever straining coarse roasted coffee grounds out of freshly brewed hot water.
Whenever separating freely mixing liquids whose boiling points sit fairly close.
Whenever settling fragile red blood cells gently away from watery yellow plasma.
Whenever harvesting dry sea-salt crystals under sunny breezes without keeping the water.
questions.explanation: Fractional distillation's repeated vaporization-condensation cycles up a tall temperature-graded column cleanly enrich mixtures of two or more volatile liquids with neighboring boiling points.

questions.prompt: Suppose Liquid X boils near $$65\,^\circ\text{C}$$ while freely mixing Liquid Y boils near $$95\,^\circ\text{C}$$. During careful fractional distillation of their mixture, what arrives at the cool top condenser first?
choices: Higher-boiling Liquid Y, because heavier vapors climb cool glass beads faster.
An unchanging fifty-fifty blend, because homogeneous solutions never boil apart.
Solid crystals of both liquids formed by rapid evaporation inside the warm pot.
Lower-boiling Liquid X, because the more volatile partner stays gaseous farthest up.
questions.explanation: As mixed vapor climbs into progressively cooler zones of the fractionating column, higher-boiling Liquid Y condenses and drips back down while more-volatile, lower-boiling Liquid X reaches the top first.

sections.title: 7. Flavor Extraction & Chromatography in Kitchen and Lab
sections.summary: Explore how selective dissolving pulls target compounds gently out of complex natural mixtures, starting with hot-water flavor extraction in espresso pucks and steeping tea leaves alongside aromatic oils infusing into warm cooking fats. Then turn that selective attraction into chromatography's continuous tug-of-war between a stay-put stationary surface and a creeping liquid solvent, watching washable black marker ink separate into colorful dye bands up wet filter paper and unmasking the golden yellows and warm oranges hiding inside green summer leaves long before autumn arrives.

chunks.title: Espresso Pucks, Steeping Tea & Solvent Extraction
chunks.content_markdown:
Toss a spoonful of table sugar into hot water and the entire spoonful disappears; toss dried green tea leaves or finely ground coffee into hot water and tough plant leaves stay solidly behind while clear water blushes amber and fragrant. That everyday selectivity powers **solvent extraction**: washing a complex raw mixture with a chosen liquid solvent that willingly dissolves target guest compounds while leaving insoluble structural bulk behind.

Every café **espresso** machine runs precision hot-water extraction in under thirty seconds! Pressurized hot water surges through a compacted puck of roasted coffee grounds, swiftly welcoming lively fruit acids, natural sugars, roasted aroma molecules, and energizing caffeine into your cup while leaving woody cellulose bean fibers behind in the knock-box. Even brew time tells a solubility story: quick soluble bright flavors leap into tea or espresso first, whereas lingering too long drags out heavy, slow-dissolving plant compounds called *tannins* that turn over-steeped tea harshly bitter and mouth-drying.

questions.prompt: When hot water steeps dried peppermint leaves in a teapot, what physical principle allows solvent extraction to flavor the cup without dissolving the whole leaf?
choices: Boiling heat melts woody plant stems temporarily into smooth green plant sap.
Teapot strainers chop intact peppermint leaves down into molecular-sized dust.
Mint flavors dissolve readily in hot water while tough woody fibers stay put.
Hot water bonds chemically with dry cellulose to create brand-new mint scents.
questions.explanation: Solvent extraction relies on selective solubility: water dissolves and lifts away soluble aroma and flavor compounds while leaving insoluble structural plant cellulose intact.

questions.prompt: Why does forgetting a black tea bag in hot water for fifteen minutes yield a mouth-drying, overly bitter mug compared with steeping for three minutes?
choices: Slow-dissolving bitter tannins keep steeping out after bright flavors finish.
Prolonged warmth evaporates sweet pure water until half the mug turns to ash.
Extended soaking pulls pleasant early aromas right back inside the wet tea bag.
Paper tea-bag fibers dissolve into sour sugars after five minutes in warm water.
questions.explanation: Different compounds inside tea leaves dissolve at different rates; pleasant lively aromatics extract quickly, whereas heavy bitter tannins keep creeping into water during prolonged steeping.

chunks.title: Matching the Solvent: Chili Oil, Vanilla & Decaf Coffee
chunks.content_markdown:
Hot water extracts tea and coffee brilliantly, yet try rinsing away the fiery tingle of a spicy jalapeño pepper with ice water and your tongue keeps right on burning—whereas a sip of milk or olive oil calms the heat promptly! Not every molecule enjoys water's company: oily, waxy flavor and scent molecules shrug off water and dissolve eagerly into oil-friendly solvents instead.

Savvy cooks match solvent to target every evening. Simmering crushed red chili flakes, garlic, or rosemary twigs gently in **olive oil** extracts rich fat-soluble color and aroma molecules that plain water would largely leave stranded inside the herb, while steeping split vanilla pods in drinkable alcohol-water spirits draws hundreds of delicate **vanilla extract** aromatics cleanly out of the bean. Food engineers even craft **decaffeinated coffee** before roasting by soaking unroasted green beans in tailored extraction fluids (such as specially handled water washes or pressurized carbon dioxide) tuned to lift caffeine selectively out while leaving prized flavor precursors behind!

questions.prompt: A chef gently warms crushed red chili peppers in olive oil rather than plain water to capture vivid red color and spicy heat for noodle bowls. Why does olive oil succeed far better?
choices: Olive oil boils much lower than water so fragile chili seeds quickly vaporize.
Water filters trap tiny spicy molecules inside invisible cages near the pot rim.
Warm olive oil freezes woody pepper skins solid so they sink cleanly downward.
Oily chili-heat and pigment molecules dissolve readily in fat solvents rather than water.
questions.explanation: Effective solvent extraction matches the solvent's particle attractions to the target solute; oil-loving chili pigments and heat compounds dissolve generously into cooking oil but poorly into water.

questions.prompt: To decaffeinate unroasted green coffee beans without turning morning coffee dull and flavorless, what special trait must the extraction solvent display?
choices: It must dissolve woody bean cellulose completely while leaving solid caffeine behind.
It must dissolve caffeine eagerly while leaving savory flavor compounds inside.
It must heat every bean well past $$100\,^\circ\text{C}$$ until dark roast oils boil away.
It must scatter bright Tyndall flashlights cleanly so workers spot floating beans.
questions.explanation: Selective extraction succeeds here by picking a solvent medium that strongly welcomes caffeine molecules out of the bean while leaving savory flavor-building compounds safely behind.

chunks.title: Color Writing & Chromatography's Friendly Tug-of-War
chunks.content_markdown:
Solvent extraction neatly lifts soluble guests away from woody solids—but once five or six different soluble dyes or plant aromas all ride dissolved side by side inside *one* tiny clear droplet, how could you ever coax them cleanly apart without boiling heat? Enter **chromatography** (from Greek roots meaning 'color writing'), a remarkably gentle separation method built around an ongoing microscopic race.

Every chromatography setup pairs two partners known as the **stationary phase and mobile phase**. The **stationary phase** is an anchored, stay-put surface with lots of microscopic nooks to cling onto (such as absorbent paper fibers or finely packed chalk powder); the **mobile phase** is a moving liquid solvent or gas flowing steadily past that surface. Caught right between them, each kind of dissolved molecule splits its time in a tug-of-war: molecules that love hugging the stationary surface linger behind in tiny steps, while molecules that strongly prefer dissolving in the flowing mobile phase sprint far ahead!

questions.prompt: In any chromatography separation, how do the stationary phase and mobile phase work together to split a dissolved mixture apart?
choices: A fluid mobile phase carries solutes past a fixed stationary surface at differing speeds.
A spinning stationary rotor flings heavy liquid mobile layers outward toward a cap.
A heated mobile burner boils frozen stationary crystals directly into chilled flasks.
A porous stationary sieve blocks big clumps while every dissolved dye exits together.
questions.explanation: Chromatography sweeps a moving fluid (mobile phase) steadily across a stay-put material (stationary phase), separating components according to how strongly each clings vs. rides along.

questions.prompt: Two dissolved food dyes start from the exact same pencil mark as water flows steadily upward across an absorbent paper strip. Dye R clings tightly to paper fibers; Dye Y strongly prefers riding in liquid water. Where do they finish?
choices: Both dyes reach the top together because homogeneous solutions never pull apart.
Paper-hugging Dye R climbs near the top while water-loving Dye Y stays down low.
Water-loving Dye Y travels high with the solvent while paper-hugging Dye R lags low.
Dye R evaporates promptly into room air while Dye Y freezes onto the starting dot.
questions.explanation: The more strongly a component favors dissolving in the moving mobile phase over clinging to the stationary phase, the bigger share of time it spends advancing—carrying Dye Y much higher.

chunks.title: Unmasking 'Black' Marker Ink on a Wet Coffee Filter
chunks.content_markdown:
You can stage a vivid chromatography race right at a kitchen table! Cut a tall strip from a white paper coffee filter (your cellulose **stationary phase**), draw a crisp dot of washable **black marker ink** a thumb's width above the bottom tip, and hang the strip so *only the very bottom edge* kisses a shallow puddle of plain tap water (**mobile phase**) sitting safely below the dry ink dot.

Immediately water wicks steadily upward between tiny paper fibers. Keep the ink above the puddle at the start so the dye doesn't simply wash downward into the cup! The moment climbing water sweeps across the black dot, the 'single' black color unpacks into a bright marching parade: rose-magenta clinging stubbornly low, sky-blue cruising calmly midway up, and eager lemon-yellow surfing right behind the wet waterline near the top! Washable 'black' ink was never a single dark compound—it was a carefully balanced mixture of colorful dye compounds exposed cleanly by differing tug-of-war loyalties.

questions.prompt: When setting up coffee-filter chromatography on an ink spot, why must the starting ink dot sit slightly *above* the shallow water puddle in the cup?
choices: Ink submerged underwater freezes paper pores shut so liquid stops climbing upward.
Submerging the ink dot washes dye down into the cup instead of up the strip.
Washable marker dyes need five minutes of dry room oxygen before turning colorful.
Liquid water acts as a mobile phase only after climbing at least one inch upward.
questions.explanation: If the starting ink dot sits below the waterline, soluble dyes dissolve straight into the bulk reservoir puddle rather than sweeping cleanly upward in sharp bands along the paper.

questions.prompt: You test two washable black markers on wet filter paper: Pen 1 stretches into distinct blue, red, and yellow bands, while Pen 2 rises cleanly as one crisp undivided dark gray spot. What is the safest conclusion?
choices: Pen 1 holds a pure element whereas Pen 2 blends three insoluble gray pigments.
Pen 1 traps boiling steam pockets whereas Pen 2 holds coarse dry sand grains.
Pen 1 reacts chemically with paper whereas Pen 2 evaporates into surrounding air.
Pen 1 mixes several distinct dyes whereas Pen 2 shows a single moving dye band.
questions.explanation: Splitting into multiple distinct bands proves Pen 1 contains multiple dye components with different stationary-vs.-mobile affinities, whereas Pen 2 reveals no multiple components under this solvent.

chunks.title: Hidden Autumn Gold Inside a Green July Leaf
chunks.content_markdown:
Chromatography shines outside the stationery drawer too—especially across parks and woodlands! Pluck a deep emerald maple or spinach leaf in mid-July, crush a bright green smear near the bottom of a filter-paper strip, and dip the tip into a shallow spoonful of household rubbing alcohol (a nimble solvent mobile phase that dissolves waxy leaf pigments far better than plain water ever could).

Watch closely over fifteen quiet minutes as alcohol creeps upward: rich green **chlorophyll** bands climb steadily partway up, while distinct ribbons of sunny golden-yellow and warm pumpkin-orange race cleanly out above the green! Deciduous trees do not manufacture all their yellow foliage from zero when October frosts roll in—many golden and orange pigments were tucked faithfully inside green leaves all summer long, visually drowned out until shorter autumn days dismantle dominant green chlorophyll! Across six sections, every phase change and separation left individual molecules completely intact; next, Section 8 asks how to recognize when particles genuinely reshuffle into brand-new substances.

questions.prompt: Running rubbing-alcohol chromatography on a deep green summer spinach leaf reveals clear yellow and orange bands climbing cleanly ahead of green bands. What does this demonstrate?
choices: Rubbing alcohol chemically scorches fresh green chlorophyll into faded autumn ash.
Green spinach leaves consist of a single pure compound that changes tint when wet.
Green summer leaves already hold hidden yellow and orange pigments masked by chlorophyll.
Yellow and orange bands come from dissolved cellulose fibers inside white filter paper.
questions.explanation: Chromatography physically separates existing mixture components without creating colors from scratch, unmasking golden-yellow and warm orange pigments already hiding beside abundant green chlorophyll.

questions.prompt: Why do food-safety and hospital labs routinely favor gentle chromatography over high-heat distillation when analyzing tiny drops of fragile vitamins or natural leaf pigments?
choices: Chromatography separates minute, heat-sensitive mixtures cleanly right at room temperature.
Chromatography destroys unwanted solvents completely so zero liquid waste stays behind.
Distillation works exclusively on chunky muddy suspensions rather than clear solutions.
Stationary surfaces turn tiny droplets into several gallons of concentrated pure water.
questions.explanation: Because chromatography sorts dissolved molecules gently via room-temperature surface-versus-solvent attractions, it separates delicate trace compounds that boiling temperatures would scorch or ruin.

sections.title: 8. Physical Change vs. Genuine Chemical Transformation
sections.summary: Draw a clear particle-level line between physical changes that rearrange spacing or shape while keeping identical particles intact—chopping onions, melting skillet butter, or dissolving salt in soup—and genuine chemical reactions that unlock reactants to forge brand-new product substances (tracked qualitatively without symbolic equation balancing or ionic formulas). Learn to weigh everyday sensory clues wisely—browning toast aromas and caramel color, baking-soda vinegar fizz, cool glowstick light, and curdled milk or soap-scum precipitates—without falling into the classic trap of mistaking rolling pasta-water steam bubbles or fizzy uncapped seltzer for bond breaking.

chunks.title: Same Molecules, New Outfit: Everyday Physical Changes
chunks.content_markdown:
Dinner prep puts half a dozen lively transformations right under your hands: slicing a crisp onion into tiny rings, melting a pat of golden butter across a warm pan, boiling kettle water into whistling vapor, and stirring snowy table salt into clear vegetable broth. Outwardly, shapes crumble, solids turn runny, and crystals disappear—yet zoom down to the particle scale and not one new kind of substance has been forged!

That anchors the calmer half of **physical change vs. chemical reaction**: a **physical change** alters a material's outward cut, phase of matter, or mixing arrangement while keeping its fundamental chemical particles intact. Melted butter still packs the exact same fat molecules; dissolved broth salt crystallizes right back out unchanged if water evaporates. Notice too why 'easy to undo' is a shaky test: you cannot magically un-dice a chopped carrot or un-crack a dropped porcelain mug, yet diced carrot is still 100% carrot! (Even with raw onions, the blade's mechanical cut is purely physical—it merely ruptures tiny cell pockets so neighboring onion fluids can meet afterward.)

questions.prompt: Grating hard parmesan cheese into fluffy shreds, melting ice cubes in lemonade, and dissolving white sugar into iced coffee look very different. Why does chemistry group all three as physical changes?
choices: All three absorb stovetop warmth steadily until reaching $$100\,^\circ\text{C}$$.
All three rearrange shape, phase, or dispersal without creating brand-new substances.
All three snap easily back to their starting shapes once left alone overnight.
All three convert heterogeneous suspensions into single pure metallic elements.
questions.explanation: Shredding a solid, melting ice, and dissolving sugar only adjust chunk size, particle spacing, or dispersal among water hosts while keeping cheese, water, and sugar identities completely unchanged.

questions.prompt: Sawing a dry pine board cleanly in half leaves fine sawdust and two shorter planks that can never seamlessly re-grow together. How should a chemist classify the cut itself?
choices: As a chemical reaction, because irreversible everyday events always forge new molecules.
As sublimation, because tiny sawdust grains float briefly through surrounding air.
As solvent extraction, because steel saw teeth pull fragrant pine oils into wood.
As a physical change, because wood chips and planks keep pine's exact molecules.
questions.explanation: Reversibility alone does not define physical change; sawing alters piece size mechanically while leaving all the natural wood compounds in both planks and sawdust chemically identical.

chunks.title: Trading Atomic Partners: Reactants, Products & Reactions
chunks.content_markdown:
Now slide pale, soft bread down into a glowing toaster, leave a bare iron garden trowel out in damp spring grass until crumbly orange rust creeps across the blade, or strike a wooden match to light a birthday candle. No coffee filter, centrifuge, cooling condenser, or chromatography strip will ever coax toasted crust back into raw dough, rust back into silvery iron by gentle drying, or candle smoke back into wax simply by chilling it!

Here you have crossed into a genuine **chemical reaction** (chemical transformation): chemical bonds holding particles together unlock and reshuffle their constituent atoms into completely *brand-new* substances displaying fresh colors, odors, melting points, and behaviors. To tell the before-and-after story cleanly without confusing guests, chemists name the starting substances entering a reaction **reactants** and the newly formed substances emerging from it **products** (**reactants and products**). On that rainy garden trowel, shiny iron metal and damp atmospheric oxygen enter as reactants; brittle, non-shiny orange rust compound emerges as the unmistakable new product.

questions.prompt: When natural gas burns cleanly on a kitchen stove by uniting invisibly with atmospheric oxygen to yield carbon dioxide gas and water vapor, which substances are the reactants and which are the products?
choices: Natural gas and oxygen are the reactants; carbon dioxide and water vapor are the products.
Carbon dioxide and water vapor are the reactants; natural gas and oxygen are the products.
Natural gas alone is the reactant; oxygen, heat, and blue flame light are the products.
Stove heat and burner steel are the reactants; warm kitchen air is the lone product.
questions.explanation: Reactants are the starting material substances consumed in a chemical transformation (natural gas and oxygen), while products are the brand-new material substances formed (carbon dioxide and water vapor).

questions.prompt: Down at the invisible particle level, what happens during a genuine chemical reaction that NEVER happens during melting, boiling, filtration, or dissolving?
choices: Whole intact molecules speed up slightly and slide farther apart from neighbors.
Matter converts entirely into weightless pure sunlight with zero mass remaining.
Starting particles unlock and rearrange their atoms to forge brand-new substances.
Intermediate clusters scatter sideways flashlight beams across a darkened glass.
questions.explanation: Physical processes move or sort whole existing particles intact, whereas chemical reactions break and remake internal chemical attachments to produce genuinely new product substances.

chunks.title: Sensory Clues I: Caramelizing Toast, Hand Warmers & Glowsticks
chunks.content_markdown:
Since we cannot watch atoms trading partners directly over breakfast, everyday chemistry relies on vivid sensory clues signaling that brand-new products just stepped onto the stage! Consider unexpected **color and aroma shifts**: warm a pan of dry white sugar past smooth clear melting into deep amber **caramel**, or brown morning toast golden-crisp, and pale odorless ingredients transform into dozens of savory, nutty, golden-brown product compounds that stay brown and fragrant long after cooling.

Watch too for spontaneous **temperature shifts or light emission** arriving with zero stove burner, refrigerator, or battery attached! Tear open an air-activated winter pocket warmer and iron powder reacting rapidly with indoor oxygen pours soothing heat into cold mittens; squeeze an athletic first-aid cold pack and an internal chemical change chills a sprained ankle on a hot field. Most magical of all, bend a plastic party **glowstick** until its inner glass tube snaps: two clear liquid reactants mingle and channel reaction energy straight into cool neon glow—the exact cold-light trick summer fireflies pull off in dusk backyards!

questions.prompt: Bending a camping glowstick cracks an inner vial so two clear room-temperature liquids mix and shine bright green light for hours without growing hot. What makes that glow strong evidence of a chemical reaction?
choices: Snapping glass filters green wavelengths out of ordinary ambient campground air.
Shaking two unmixable oils produces bright green Tyndall headlight scattering.
Sublimating dry plastic releases stored noon sunlight trapped inside the tube.
Mixing reactants spontaneously emits new light energy as fresh products form.
questions.explanation: Continuous spontaneous light emission triggered solely by mixing two cool liquids without any external bulb or battery signals a chemical reaction forging brand-new products.

questions.prompt: Warming white table sugar gently first turns clear and runny (Stage 1), then darker heating turns it rich amber with toasted butterscotch aroma that never turns white again on cooling (Stage 2). How do the stages compare?
choices: Both stages are strictly physical phase changes from solid crystal into liquid.
Stage 1 melts intact sugar physically; Stage 2 reacts it into caramel products.
Stage 1 splits sugar chemically apart; Stage 2 condenses brown vapor back down.
Both stages are chemical reactions driven by pulling nitrogen from kitchen air.
questions.explanation: Initial clear melting keeps sugar molecules intact (physical change), whereas darkening color and rich new caramel aromas reflect irreversible breakdown and reassembly into brand-new compounds.

chunks.title: Sensory Clues II: Vinegar Fizz & Curdling Precipitates
chunks.content_markdown:
Two more dramatic kitchen clues announce themselves whenever room-temperature reactants build a brand-new product belonging to a *different state of matter*! Spoon tangy liquid vinegar onto dry white baking soda (or drop a fizzy antacid tablet into still tap water), and exuberant **gas fizz** foams right over the rim without any stove flame underneath—because vinegar acid and baking soda unlock and trade parts to create brand-new gaseous carbon dioxide right inside cool water.

Just as striking is the sudden birth of an insoluble solid called a **precipitate** when two liquids meet! Squeeze clear sour lemon juice into warm homogenized milk while crafting fresh kitchen paneer or ricotta cheese, and acid reacts with milk proteins so smooth dairy abruptly knots into snowy solid curds floating in pale greenish whey. The same uninvited chemistry greets anyone lathering classic bar soap in mineral-heavy 'hard' tap water: dissolved calcium and magnesium minerals react instantly with dissolved soap molecules to drop a gray, insoluble film of bathtub soap-scum precipitate!

questions.prompt: When washing hands with traditional bar soap in mineral-rich tap water leaves a cloudy, insoluble gray ring of soap scum that refuses to rinse clear, what chemical term describes that newly formed solid?
choices: A volatile distillate condensed out of warm bathroom shower vapor.
A pure metallic alloy cooled rapidly against cold porcelain walls.
An insoluble precipitate formed as soap reacts with tap-water minerals.
A saturated host solvent left behind after excess pure water evaporates.
questions.explanation: When dissolved reactants react inside a liquid to forge a brand-new insoluble solid compound that separates from solution (like bathtub soap scum or curdled cheese), chemists call that solid a precipitate.

questions.prompt: Stirring cool lemon juice into baking-soda pancake batter fills the batter with tiny bubbles well before it touches a warm griddle. Where do those bubbles come from?
choices: Acid and baking soda react chemically to generate brand-new carbon dioxide gas.
Cold lemon water boils vigorously into steam pockets upon meeting dry white flour.
Whisking heats milk fat past its saturation ceiling until butter sublimates out.
Filter pores inside flour grains release compressed room helium during wet mixing.
questions.explanation: Spontaneous fizzing when cool baking soda meets sour lemon juice signals a genuine chemical reaction generating brand-new carbon dioxide gas bubbles that puff up fluffy pancakes.

chunks.title: Dodging the Bubble Trap: Boiling Pasta vs. Breaking Bonds
chunks.content_markdown:
Here comes the sharpest kitchen-detective rule of the entire section: *sensory clues invite investigation, but one clue taken out of context can easily fool you!* Nowhere do people slip faster than with **bubbles**. Set a bubbly mug of vinegar-and-baking-soda beside a rolling pot of boiling pure pasta water and a freshly uncapped bottle of warm seltzer. All three fizz or churn with rising gas pockets—yet only *one* is a chemical reaction!

Inside boiling pasta water, stovetop heat simply pries intact water molecules apart into rising steam vapor (a pure physical phase change—condense that vapor on a cool pot lid and plain liquid water drips right back!). Inside uncapped seltzer, dropping bottle pressure lets *already existing* dissolved carbon dioxide molecules un-dissolve physically out of water. Even stirring blue paint into yellow paint makes green purely by physical side-by-side light absorption rather than reacting! Always check the single decisive test: did starting atoms reshuffle into a *genuinely new substance*? Next, when wood and candles truly react into invisible gases, Section 9 places the whole blaze onto Lavoisier's balance!

questions.prompt: Four everyday containers bubble actively on a kitchen counter. Which container is undergoing a genuine chemical reaction rather than a purely physical change?
choices: Pure distilled water churning at a steady rolling boil inside an electric kettle.
Crushed antacid tablet fizzing briskly after dropping into room-temperature tap water.
Chilled plain sparkling seltzer foaming gently right after someone twists off the cap.
Clear ice water releasing tiny pinpoint bubbles of dissolved air as the glass warms up.
questions.explanation: Boiling water vaporizes intact water molecules and warming/uncapping seltzer or tap water merely releases already-present dissolved gases; only the fizzing antacid tablet chemically forges brand-new carbon dioxide gas.

questions.prompt: A friend watches big bubbles burst across boiling spaghetti water at $$100\,^\circ\text{C}$$ and remarks, 'Look at the stove breaking water molecules apart into hydrogen and oxygen gas!' What corrects that misconception?
choices: Boiling actually fuses two water molecules together into heavier liquid drops.
Water splits at $$100\,^\circ\text{C}$$ into carbon dioxide gas rather than hydrogen and oxygen.
Spaghetti starch acts as a stationary phase absorbing oxygen before bubbles pop.
Boiling loosens attractions between intact water molecules so steam is still pure water.
questions.explanation: Stovetop boiling overcomes gentle neighbor-to-neighbor attractions without touching the strong internal chemical bonds inside each water molecule—catching the rising steam on a cool lid returns pure water.

sections.title: 9. Lavoisier's Sealed Flasks & Conservation of Mass
sections.summary: Unravel why campfires and dinner candles look as if they destroy matter into tiny heaps of ash while damp outdoor iron grows mysteriously heavier as it rusts—both illusions created by invisible gases entering or escaping an open system. Step into Antoine and Marie-Anne Lavoisier's tightly sealed glass flasks to see why weighing trapped oxygen, vapors, and solids together leaves total mass completely unchanged across any reaction, then apply that same mass-conservation intuition qualitatively to discover why human weight lost overnight exits your body mainly through your lungs as exhaled carbon dioxide and water vapor.

chunks.title: Vanishing Logs, Heavy Rust & Open vs. Closed Systems
chunks.content_markdown:
Stack hefty dry oak logs onto an evening campfire and by morning only a featherlight scoop of gray ash remains; burn a tall beeswax candle through dinner and the solid pillar shrinks steadily into thin air. Yet leave a bare iron horseshoe outdoors in damp spring weather, and weighing it after rust coats the metal reveals the rusty shoe grew noticeably *heavier*! How could burning seem to erase matter while rusting quietly creates extra mass out of nowhere?

Both everyday riddles trace straight back to untracked invisible gas traffic across an **open vs. closed system**. An **open system**—such as a backyard firepit, a tabletop candlestick, or an unstoppered kitchen bowl—lets matter (especially unseen gases and vapors) wander freely in from surrounding air or drift freely away unweighed. Seal that exact process inside a rigid, leak-proof glass vessel, and you establish a **closed system**: warmth and light still travel freely through clear glass walls, yet not a single particle of solid, liquid, or gas can sneak across the boundary!

questions.prompt: Why did ordinary backyard campfires convince observers for centuries that roaring flames literally wipe solid matter out of existence?
choices: High flame temperatures convert solid wood logs completely into weightless orange light.
Campfire ash particles pack so tightly together that standard scales misread their mass.
Open firepits let bulky gaseous reaction products drift invisibly away into surrounding air.
Wood contains mostly trapped sunlight accompanied by only a tiny pinch of solid ash.
questions.explanation: An outdoor campfire is an open system; most of the reacted matter leaves quietly as invisible gases and rising vapor rather than remaining behind in the small mineral ash pile.

questions.prompt: When studying a fizzing or burning transformation in a lab, what strictly separates a closed system from an open system?
choices: A closed system keeps all matter sealed inside while still letting heat or light pass.
A closed system blocks light and warmth completely while letting excess gas vent safely.
A closed system permits only physical phase changes and halts every chemical reaction.
A closed system replaces ordinary room air with solid sand so nothing moves inside.
questions.explanation: Energy like heat and light can still cross the walls of a typical closed glass flask, but its leak-tight seal prevents any solid, liquid, or gaseous matter from entering or escaping.

chunks.title: Inside Lavoisier's Precision Balances & Sealed Glass Flasks
chunks.content_markdown:
In late-eighteenth-century Paris, Antoine Lavoisier and his indispensable scientific partner Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier cracked the ancient riddle of fire and rust by pairing extraordinarily sensitive balances with melted-shut glass flasks. Lavoisier placed weighed shiny metal inside a glass flask filled with ordinary air, sealed the glass neck completely airtight, weighed the entire closed bulb, and heated it steadily until a dull powdery crust coated the metal.

When the cooled, still-sealed flask returned to the balance pan, the pointer sat dead steady—the *total mass* of glass, crusty metal, and remaining trapped air had not budged by the tiniest hair! Yet when Lavoisier finally snapped open the sealed glass neck, outside room air hissed sharply *inward*, raising the flask's reading by the exact extra mass the crusty metal had gained! Nothing materialized from thin air during heating: the metal had simply locked onto invisible **oxygen** gas already sealed inside the bulb, slimming the trapped air by the identical mass added to the solid metal–oxygen compound crust.

questions.prompt: After Lavoisier heated shiny tin or mercury inside a hermetically sealed, air-filled glass flask until a powdery crust formed, what did weighing the cooled, unopened flask reveal?
choices: Total flask mass climbed steadily because absorbed stove heat added solid weight.
Total flask mass dropped slightly because crusty powder weighed less than metal.
Total flask mass swung unpredictably depending on afternoon humidity outside.
Total flask mass matched its starting value identically down to balance precision.
questions.explanation: Because the sealed glass flask formed a closed system, oxygen locking chemically onto the solid metal stayed fully contained inside without altering the flask's total combined mass.

questions.prompt: Why does an unpainted iron garden gate weigh slightly *more* on a sensitive scale after rusting outside all spring (assuming none of the flaky rust falls off)?
choices: Cold spring rainwater freezes permanently inside solid gray iron atoms.
Rusting locks formerly unweighed oxygen from outdoor air into the solid crust.
Sunlight slows iron particle motion down so Earth's gravity pulls harder.
Chemical reactions naturally manufacture slight bonus mass inside sturdy metals.
questions.explanation: Left outdoors in an open system, shiny iron combines chemically with invisible atmospheric oxygen (and moisture); weighing the rusty gate afterward now includes that captured oxygen mass.

chunks.title: Unmasking Candle & Campfire Combustion
chunks.content_markdown:
Once Lavoisier recognized oxygen gas as a full-fledged material reactant with real mass, burning ceased to look like mysterious destruction. Chemists call rapid, heat-and-light-releasing reaction between a fuel and oxygen gas **combustion**.

Follow a glowing dinner candle with particle eyes! Solid candle wax (like dry campfire wood or stove gas) is built chiefly from chemically bonded carbon and hydrogen. As warm melted wax climbs the wick into the flame, it doesn't vanish into weightless orange light: its carbon and hydrogen unlock and combine briskly with invisible room **oxygen** to escape upward as two colorless gaseous products—**carbon dioxide** gas and **water vapor**! You can catch one invisible product right at the dinner table: hold the back of a cold metal soup spoon well above a small candle flame for two seconds (never touching the soot zone), and a delicate fog of clear liquid water condenses straight out of the rising combustion plume!

questions.prompt: As a tall taper candle burns steadily down to a tiny stub during a holiday dinner, what happened to almost all of the missing wax matter?
choices: It united with room oxygen and left as invisible carbon dioxide and water vapor.
It converted directly into flickering yellow candlelight and radiant dining-room heat.
It soaked gradually downward through the solid brass candleholder onto the table.
It sublimated intact so solid wax molecules now hover unchanged near the ceiling.
questions.explanation: During candle combustion, carbon and hydrogen from the wax unite chemically with atmospheric oxygen to form colorless gaseous carbon dioxide and water vapor that disperse into the room.

questions.prompt: When natural gas burns cleanly on a blue kitchen burner beneath a cold kettle on a crisp winter morning, faint moisture briefly mists the chilly kettle bottom before clearing. Where did that water come from?
choices: Liquid tap water sweated directly outward through solid stainless-steel walls.
Cold burner pipes condensed dry nitrogen out of ordinary indoor kitchen air.
Combustion united hydrogen from the fuel gas with room oxygen into fresh water vapor.
Blue stovetop flames melted frost stored deep inside cast-iron burner grates.
questions.explanation: Fuel gases contain bonded hydrogen; burning them with atmospheric oxygen chemically creates hot gaseous water vapor as a major combustion product, which briefly condenses against the cold kettle.

chunks.title: Nothing Conjured, Nothing Lost: Conservation of Mass
chunks.content_markdown:
Repeated across thousands of careful closed-container experiments—melting ice, dissolving salt, precipitating cheese curds, rusting wet steel wool, or burning a tiny candle inside a large oxygen-filled glass globe—nature gives the exact same unyielding answer enshrined as the **Law of Conservation of Mass**: in every physical change and ordinary chemical reaction, matter is neither created nor destroyed, so the total combined mass of all **products** always equals the exact total combined mass of all **reactants** consumed.

Picture dropping a fizzing antacid tablet into half a bottle of water twice on a digital kitchen scale. Leave the plastic cap *off* (open system), and the gram display quietly ticks down as newly formed carbon dioxide fizz slips away into room air. Twist a sturdy soda-bottle cap *tightly shut* first (closed system), let the whole tablet fizz away inside, and the scale number sits rock-solid from start to finish—because trapped gas pushing inside the firm bottle still presses downward with every bit of its conserved mass!

questions.prompt: You mix vinegar and baking soda inside a sturdy, tightly capped plastic soda bottle resting undisturbed on a kitchen balance. As the powder reacts and the bottle firms up with gas, what does the balance display do?
choices: It drops noticeably because gases stay completely weightless once unleashed.
It remains completely unchanged because all reactant and product matter stays trapped.
It climbs steadily higher because fizzing creates brand-new gas mass from pressure.
It dips during fizzing and rebounds only after you twist the bottle cap open.
questions.explanation: Inside a rigid, leak-tight closed bottle, every trace of newly formed carbon dioxide gas stays contained alongside the liquid, so total mass stays identical from start to finish.

questions.prompt: Suppose you next loosen that tight bottle cap slowly until trapped fizz hisses gently out into the kitchen without spilling a single drop of liquid. What happens on the balance right then, and why?
choices: The reading jumps up slightly because fresh room nitrogen rushes inside to sink.
The reading holds completely flat because colorless gases possess zero measurable mass.
The reading drops briefly from cold air currents, then returns to its sealed value.
The reading ticks down slightly because escaping gas carries real mass away.
questions.explanation: Gases are genuine matter with real mass; uncapping switches the bottle to an open system, allowing gaseous carbon dioxide product to exit unweighed into the room.

chunks.title: Where Overnight Sleeping Weight Loss Really Goes
chunks.content_markdown:
Now step onto an accurate bathroom scale right before climbing into bed, sleep eight restful hours without eating, sipping water, or visiting the bathroom, and weigh yourself first thing at sunrise: you reliably wake up noticeably *lighter*! Even across months of hiking and healthy eating when someone loses ten pounds, folks casually say they 'burned fat off into body heat and energy.' Yet Lavoisier smiles politely and shakes his head: body heat is mass-free thermal energy—you cannot turn pounds of physical atoms into pure warmth!

All night long (and faster while jogging), your cells run gentle, flame-free biological fuel combustion: combining stored carbon-and-hydrogen food molecules with inhaled **oxygen** gas to power heartbeats and warmth while assembling two overwhelmingly familiar waste products—**carbon dioxide** gas and **water**! Besides faint skin perspiration evaporation, the massive majority of overnight (and exercise!) weight loss rides calmly right out through your nose and mouth as invisible exhaled carbon dioxide and warm breath moisture! Next, Section 10 closes our journey with Proust and Dalton's astonishing discovery hidden inside conserved mass ratios.

questions.prompt: During eight peaceful hours of sleep with zero trips to the kitchen or bathroom, your body becomes measurably lighter by morning. How did the bulk of those lost atoms physically exit your body?
choices: They radiated directly through cotton blankets as weightless infrared body heat.
They compacted tighter inside muscle fibers so gravity pulled gently weaker.
They exited mostly via your lungs and skin as exhaled carbon dioxide and water vapor.
They stayed fully inside your bloodstream while warm air made the bathroom buoyant.
questions.explanation: Conservation of mass requires lost body weight to exit as real matter: gentle cellular fuel burning pairs stored carbon and hydrogen with inhaled oxygen and exhales them primarily as carbon dioxide gas and water vapor.

questions.prompt: Why does the everyday fitness phrase 'my brisk morning hike turned body fat straight into pure motion energy and warmth' miss the key lesson of Lavoisier's balance?
choices: Energy lacks mass, so lost fat atoms exit your body as exhaled gas and moisture.
Human muscles run strictly on physical phase changes without any chemical reactions occurring.
Body fat behaves like rusting iron and always grows heavier whenever extra oxygen enters lungs.
Closed human skin traps every reacted carbon particle permanently until hair gets trimmed.
questions.explanation: While reacting stored fat with oxygen releases the energy powering movement and body warmth, the physical carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms strictly conserve mass and exit primarily through exhaled breath and moisture.

sections.title: 10. Definite Proportions, Multiple Proportions & Dalton's Atoms
sections.summary: Crown the module by connecting macroscopic weighing scales back to individual countable particles through effortless small-integer intuition rather than stoichiometry math. Contrast Proust's fixed mass recipe inside every pure compound (such as pure water's unwavering $$8:1$$ oxygen-to-hydrogen mass ratio regardless of source) with Dalton's breakthrough comparison of two distinct carbon-and-oxygen gases—where doubling the oxygen mass per fixed share of carbon in a crisp $$2:1$$ whole-number jump proves matter is built from discrete, indestructible atoms that pair in clean whole numbers and reshuffle during reactions—before handing off warmly to Part II's exploration of what lies inside the atom itself.

chunks.title: Nature's Unbending Recipe Book: Proust & Definite Proportions
chunks.content_markdown:
When you sweeten morning coffee or stir vinaigrette, you play carefree chef—a tiny splash more lemon or sugar smoothly tweaks the mixture. Right around 1799, meticulous French chemist Joseph Proust proved that genuine pure **compounds** behave nothing like kitchen mixtures! Under Proust's **Law of Definite Proportions** (also called constant composition), every pure sample of a given chemical compound always contains the exact same elements locked together in one *strict, unchanging ratio by mass*—regardless of its geographic origin or how it was made.

Take pure distilled water from anywhere on Earth—thawed from ancient Antarctic glacier ice, condensed from tropical rainforest mist, or synthesized fresh from pure gases in a classroom bulb. Split those pure samples carefully apart and weigh the collected gases: every single sample yields precisely eight parts of oxygen mass for every one part of hydrogen mass—an unbudging $$8:1$$ mass recipe! Try forcing extra leftover hydrogen into the spark bulb once all oxygen is spoken for, and nature politely leaves the spare hydrogen untouched beside ordinary $$8:1$$ water.

questions.prompt: One bottle of completely pure distilled water comes from boiled-and-condensed Pacific seawater, while a second comes from melted Swiss mountain snow. According to Proust's Law of Definite Proportions, how do they compare?
choices: Ocean-derived pure water carries slightly extra oxygen mass from salty sea breezes.
Both pure samples lock oxygen to hydrogen in the exact same $$8:1$$ mass ratio.
Snow-derived pure water holds extra hydrogen mass because mountain air sits thinner.
Only laboratory-synthesized water follows $$8:1$$ while natural waters vary smoothly.
questions.explanation: Once purified free of mixture impurities, every sample of a single chemical compound like pure water exhibits the exact same fixed element-to-element mass ratio regardless of source.

questions.prompt: If pure table salt is a true chemical compound obeying the Law of Definite Proportions, what distinguishes it immediately from a saltwater true solution?
choices: Pure table salt adjusts its element proportions flexibly depending on stove heat.
Saltwater locks water onto salt in one single unchangeable global mass ratio.
Pure table salt scatters bright Tyndall cones whenever dissolved cleanly in water.
Pure table salt keeps one unvarying element mass ratio whereas saltwater mixes flexibly.
questions.explanation: A mixture like saltwater accepts flexible solute-to-solvent recipes right up to saturation, whereas pure table salt itself is a compound whose bonded elements never deviate from one fixed mass ratio.

chunks.title: Same Two Elements, Two Utterly Different Everyday Gases
chunks.content_markdown:
Proust's fixed recipe raises a natural next curiosity: if pure carbon and pure oxygen lock together strictly by rule, can those same two elements ever team up in *more than one* distinct way to build two completely different compounds? Winter safety detectors in millions of hallways answer with an emphatic *yes*!

Burn dry charcoal in plenty of fresh outdoor air (or simply breathe out, or uncork sparkling seltzer), and carbon teams up generously with oxygen to form familiar, nonflammable **carbon dioxide**—the harmless gas plants drink in to build green leaves and bakers count on to puff bread dough. Yet smolder that exact same charcoal inside a closed garage starved of oxygen, and carbon links up in a leaner partnership to forge a *totally separate* pure compound: silent, odorless, dangerously poisonous **carbon monoxide** gas (which itself can still burn further with a pale blue flame!). Both gases contain nothing whatsoever besides carbon and oxygen—and *each* individual compound loyally keeps its own strict Proust recipe.

questions.prompt: Carbon monoxide is a toxic, flammable gas whereas carbon dioxide safely puts bubbles in seltzer and smothers fires—yet both consist solely of bonded carbon and oxygen. How does chemistry reconcile that?
choices: They are two distinct pure compounds, each locking carbon and oxygen in its own fixed ratio.
They are identical molecules simply moving at hot versus chilled average speeds.
Carbon monoxide is a loose heterogeneous suspension of black soot floating in air.
Carbon dioxide contains added room nitrogen to calm down toxic carbon atoms.
questions.explanation: The same pair of elements can form two genuinely distinct chemical compounds with dramatically different fixed compositions—and therefore totally different physical, chemical, and physiological traits.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't the existence of both carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide break Proust's Law of Definite Proportions?
choices: Proust's law applies exclusively to liquid water and solid minerals rather than gases.
Carbon slowly shifts smoothly across every possible ratio between the two gases.
Every pure sample of either specific gas still holds its own unvarying mass ratio.
Open flames temporarily suspend Proust's law whenever winter air runs low.
questions.explanation: Proust's law governs each specific compound individually: pure carbon monoxide always holds one fixed carbon-to-oxygen ratio, and pure carbon dioxide always holds its own distinct fixed ratio.

chunks.title: Whole Eggs, Not Poured Batter: Dalton's $$2:1$$ Ratio Leap
chunks.content_markdown:
Around 1803 in rainy Manchester, observant teacher and meteorologist John Dalton laid the fixed mass recipes of sibling compounds like carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide side by side—and noticed a jaw-dropping pattern hiding in plain sight! Suppose you take a pure sample of carbon monoxide and a pure sample of carbon dioxide chosen so both hold the *exact same mass of carbon*. Now compare the mass of oxygen partnered to that identical share of carbon in each gas: carbon dioxide carries **precisely twice** the mass of oxygen found in carbon monoxide—a crystal-clean $$2:1$$ whole-number step, never a messy fraction like $$1.73:1$$ or $$2.14:1$$!

Checked across nitrogen–oxygen gases, iron–oxygen minerals, and copper–oxygen powders, the **Law of Multiple Proportions** held everywhere: whenever two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other always form ratios of *small whole numbers*! Picture baking two cakes over identical bowls of flour: poured milk yields any random decimal ratio, whereas cracking intact *whole eggs* cleanly gives two eggs versus one egg—a telltale $$2:1$$ jump screaming 'countable units inside!'

questions.prompt: Comparing equal carbon shares in pure carbon dioxide versus pure carbon monoxide always yields a crisp $$2:1$$ jump in combined oxygen mass rather than an awkward decimal like $$1.87:1$$. What huge clue does that clean whole number give?
choices: Gases expand to double their volume whenever warmed slightly past room temperature.
Laboratory balances round every awkward gas weight politely to the nearest integer.
Continuous smooth fluids naturally divide themselves in half when stirred gently.
Oxygen joins carbon in discrete, countable whole units rather than continuous smears.
questions.explanation: Just as whole eggs added to identical bowls of flour double cleanly in a $$2:1$$ step without half-or-decimal smears, small whole-number mass jumps reveal matter combines in discrete countable pieces.

questions.prompt: Which comparison specifically showcases Dalton's Law of Multiple Proportions in action?
choices: Noting that pure Arctic snowmelt and pure kettle distillate share water's $$8:1$$ recipe.
Finding a $$2:1$$ copper mass step across two distinct pure copper–oxygen compounds.
Stirring twice as much sugar into Mug A of hot tea compared with Mug B of hot tea.
Weighing a sealed glass flask before and after burning fuel and finding equal total mass.
questions.explanation: Definite proportions checks different samples of *one* compound (Arctic vs. kettle water); multiple proportions compares *two distinct compounds* forged from the same two elements (yielding clean steps like $$2:1$$).

chunks.title: Everything Clicks Together: Dalton's Atomic Theory
chunks.content_markdown:
With one brilliant stroke—**Dalton's atomic theory**—John Dalton showed how a single clean particle picture explains Lavoisier's conserved mass, Proust's fixed recipes, and his own $$2:1$$ jumps all at once! Dalton proposed that every element is built from tiny, discrete, indestructible particles called **atoms**: every copper atom shares copper's characteristic mass, every carbon atom shares carbon's mass, and every oxygen atom shares oxygen's mass.

Watch all three laws snap effortlessly into place like puzzle tiles! First, because chemical reactions never conjure, erase, or chop half an atom—they merely unsnap and reshuffle intact whole atoms into fresh partnerships—total mass is automatically conserved (**Lavoisier**). Second, if pure water always attaches oxygen and hydrogen atoms in one unchanging partnership and each element's atoms carry fixed characteristic mass, pure water's macroscopic mass ratio can never stray from $$8:1$$ (**Proust**). Third, if carbon monoxide pairs each carbon atom with *one* oxygen atom while carbon dioxide pairs each carbon atom with *two* oxygen atoms, oxygen's mass per fixed carbon steps up in an effortless, exact $$2:1$$ jump (**Dalton**)!

questions.prompt: Through the lens of Dalton's atomic theory, why does pure carbon dioxide hold exactly twice the mass of oxygen per fixed amount of carbon compared with pure carbon monoxide ($$2:1$$)?
choices: Each oxygen atom inside carbon dioxide swells cleanly to double its ordinary mass.
Carbon monoxide slices every oxygen atom neatly in half during smoky burning.
Each carbon atom partners with two whole oxygen atoms instead of just one.
Carbon dioxide traps an extra pocket of unbonded room air between molecules.
questions.explanation: Because every oxygen atom carries the same characteristic mass, pairing two intact oxygen atoms per carbon atom automatically delivers exactly twice the oxygen mass of pairing one oxygen atom per carbon atom.

questions.prompt: According to Dalton's atomic theory, why is it completely impossible for an ordinary sealed-flask bonfire or vinegar-fizz reaction to gain or lose even a trace of total mass?
choices: Reactions only rearrange the exact same inventory of intact, indestructible atoms.
Released flame heat carries just enough mass to replace every destroyed carbon atom.
Atoms pause all internal jiggling motion the moment chemical bonding finishes.
Every reactant atom transforms smoothly into an equal weight of liquid water.
questions.explanation: If zero atoms are created, destroyed, or altered in individual mass while swapping bonding partners inside a sealed flask, counting the exact same intact atoms afterward guarantees identical total mass.

chunks.title: Kitchen Chemistry Unified & Looking Inside the Atom Next
chunks.content_markdown:
Pause at your kitchen counter and admire how far your intuition now reaches without memorizing a single dense equation! One warm, visual picture of countable moving particles ties everything effortlessly together: locked ice melting through sliding liquid into $$100\,^\circ\text{C}$$ boiling pasta vapor while fast-escaping sweat molecules cool summer skin; pure copper pans and $$8:1$$ water compounds distinguished cleanly from stainless steel, sweet tea solutions, glowing Tyndall milk colloids, and settling muddy suspensions; coffee filters, blood centrifuges, distillation condensers, and ascending leaf-pigment chromatograms rescuing intact ingredients; and caramelizing toast, exhaled sleeping breaths, and Dalton's $$2:1$$ ratios revealing indestructible atoms trading partners cleanly!

Yet Dalton left a tantalizing mystery sitting right on the windowsill. Picturing atoms as tiny, solid, indivisible billiard balls beautifully explained *how* we count mass—while leaving wide open *what hides inside an atom* to make shiny copper utterly unlike breathable oxygen, help salt hug water, or snap atoms into sturdy molecules! In **Everyday Chemical Foundations II**, we step gently inside Dalton's atom at this exact unhurried pace.

questions.prompt: Stepping back across our entire everyday toolkit, which trio of household processes leaves every original compound molecule completely un-reshuffled from start to finish?
choices: Toasting bread brown, snapping a party glowstick, and burning a beeswax candle.
Boiling pasta water, distilling salty seawater, and separating ink by chromatography.
Curdling warm milk with lemon, rusting damp iron, and fizzing baking soda in vinegar.
Caramelizing white sugar, exhaling overnight breath gas, and burning stove gas.
questions.explanation: Boiling, distillation, and paper chromatography rely purely on physical phase changes and selective surface-vs.-solvent attractions, leaving every original molecule intact without breaking or making chemical bonds.

questions.prompt: Dalton's billiard-ball picture of countable, indestructible atoms triumphed at explaining reaction mass laws, yet left which big question unanswered for Part II?
choices: Whether gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide truly possess measurable mass and volume.
Whether mixtures like seawater can ever be separated cleanly by simple boiling.
Whether boiling pure water past $$100\,^\circ\text{C}$$ destroys mass inside a sealed glass flask.
What internal structure gives different elements distinct traits and drives atoms to bond.
questions.explanation: Treating atoms as solid, featureless spheres explained mass conservation and whole-number ratios wonderfully, while setting up Part II's discovery of the internal atomic architecture behind distinct elements and chemical bonding.
